items.prose:
Your home folder /Users/ana holds data and projects. You run:

```sh
$ pwd
/Users/ana/data
$ cd ../projects
$ pwd
```
items.question: What does the second `pwd` print?

options.why: You went down from data. The two dots first climb out of data, up to ana.
You stopped after the two dots. The path carries on down into projects.
pwd never prints a relative path. It prints the full path from /.

feedback.correct: Up to ana, then down into projects.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read ../projects one piece at a time from data.

explain.text: `..` climbs from data to ana, then projects steps down. pwd prints the full path: /Users/ana/projects.

items.prose:
Your broker's exports folder holds these files:

```sh
$ ls
positions_mar.csv  trades_feb.csv  trades_jan.csv
trades_mar.csv     trades_summary.txt
```

You run `cp trades_*.csv ~/projects/backtest/data/`.
items.question: How many files are copied?

feedback.correct: Three names start with trades_ and end in .csv.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A name must match both ends of the pattern.

byKey.summary: You counted trades_summary.txt. It starts right but ends in .txt, so the pattern skips it. positions_mar.csv ends right but starts wrong.
byKey.everything: You copied every file. The pattern names a start and an end, and only three files fit both.

explain.text: The pattern needs trades_ at the start and .csv at the end. trades_jan, trades_feb and trades_mar fit. trades_summary.txt fails at the end and positions_mar.csv at the start.

items.prose:
A day's fills are saved in fills.csv:

```sh
$ cat fills.csv
time,ticker,side,qty
09:30,AAPL,buy,100
09:31,MSFT,sell,50
09:45,AAPL,sell,100
10:02,NVDA,buy,20
10:15,AAPL,buy,40
$ grep buy fills.csv | wc -l
```
items.question: What number does the last command print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lines grep passes to wc.

byKey.file: You counted the whole file. After the pipe, wc only sees grep's output.
byKey.aapl: You counted only the Apple buys. grep buy keeps every line containing buy.
byKey.header: You added the header. It contains side, not buy, so grep drops it.

explain.text: grep keeps the AAPL, NVDA and AAPL buy lines. The pipe passes those three lines to wc, which prints 3.

options.text: An argument: the folder ls works on
An option that changes how ls behaves
options.why: Options start with a dash. ~/Downloads has none, so it names what to list.
There is only one command, ls, the first word. The rest is options and arguments.

feedback.correct: It names what ls works on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the dash.

explain.text: ls is the command, -lt two options squeezed together, and ~/Downloads the argument. So ls lists Downloads in long form, newest first.

items.prose: You are in ~/data, which holds prices.csv and notes.txt.
items.question: Which commands lose data with no way back? Select all that apply.

options.why: mkdir only adds an empty folder. It never touches what exists.
ls only reads. It changes nothing.

feedback.correct: Both rm commands, and the redirect onto its own input.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for anything that deletes or empties a file.

byKey.self: You missed the redirect. The shell empties prices.csv before grep reads it, so grep finds nothing and the file stays empty.

explain.text: rm and rm -r delete for good. The redirect is sneakier: `>` empties prices.csv before grep starts, so grep reads an empty file. Never redirect a command into the file it is reading.

items.prose: Your folder holds data.csv and data_old.csv, and nothing else starting with d. You type `head da` and press Tab once.
items.question: What happens?

options.text: The line becomes `head data` and waits, because two names match
It picks data.csv, the first match
options.why: Tab never guesses between names. It fills in only what every match shares.
Tab ignores dates. It fills in only what every match shares.

options.text: Nothing, because Tab only works on folders

feedback.correct: Tab fills in the shared part, data, then waits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what both names have in common.

explain.text: Both names start with data, then differ: a dot in one, an underscore in the other. Tab fills in data and stops. A second Tab lists both, and you type one more character to choose.

items.prose: A folder holds three exports. Here are their names and when each last changed.
items.question: What does `ls -t | head -1` print?

options.why: That is first alphabetically, which plain ls gives. -t sorts by time, newest first.
18:10 is the latest clock time, but on 4 June. The 5 June file is newer.

feedback.correct: The 5 June export is the newest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the dates first, then the times.

explain.text: ls -t lists export_b, export_c, then export_a. head -1 keeps the first line: export_b.csv.

items.prose:
all.csv already holds the 3 AAPL lines from prices.csv, which also has 3 MSFT lines. You run:

```sh
$ grep MSFT prices.csv >> all.csv
$ wc -l all.csv
```
items.question: What number does `wc -l` print?

widget.label: Line count
widget.accept: 6: the 3 AAPL lines, then the 3 MSFT lines

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `>>` adds to the end of the file.

byKey.replaced: You treated `>>` like `>`. A double sign adds to the end and keeps what was there.
byKey.file: all.csv never had the header. It holds AAPL lines and MSFT lines only.

explain.text: `>>` appends, so the 3 MSFT lines join the 3 AAPL lines. wc counts 6. With a single `>` the AAPL lines would have been wiped.
